chapter.name: State and Society up to 1000 CE

questions.q: In a Rajasthan town, neighbours by long habit send food to a family that has lost a member; no rule or officer requires it. The same town's market committee fines a shop that uses a false weight, and an inspector checks the scales. Which description fits the chapter's ideas of society and State?
questions.a: The food custom belongs to society; the fine rests on rules and enforcement, so it belongs to the State. The chapter says society is regulated primarily by customs and practices, while a State is an organised political system based on rules and laws with institutions to enforce them.
o: The food custom belongs to society; the fine rests on rules and enforcement, so it belongs to the State
The food custom belongs to the State; the fine is only a custom of the traders, so it belongs to society
Both belong to society, because everyone in the town shares a territory and a culture
Both belong to the State, because any practice that keeps order is made by rulers

questions.q: Ananya's teacher says the Rigveda is our best early literary evidence because the script of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation has not been deciphered. Which reason from the chapter best supports this?
questions.a: It is the earliest known body of literature, filling the gap the script leaves. The chapter calls the Vedas the earliest known corpus of Indian literature, says they existed in oral form for centuries before being written, and says the date of the Rigveda is debated.
o: It is the earliest known body of literature, filling the gap the script leaves
The Rigveda was written down on the day it was composed, so it records exact dates
The Rigveda was composed in the Ganga plains, so it describes the Harappan cities directly
Its date is agreed by all historians, so no other source is needed

questions.q: Ishaan reads one text that explains how rituals are performed, in prose, and another that reflects on the Self (Atman) and the Ultimate Universal Being (Brahman). Which parts of a Veda is he reading, in that order?
questions.a: Brahmana, then Upanishad. The Brahmana, in prose, explain ritual performances; the Upanishads deal with the Self and the Ultimate Universal Being. Samhitas hold hymns and Aranyakas expand on the speculations of forest sages.
o: Brahmana, then Upanishad
Samhita, then Aranyaka
Aranyaka, then Samhita
Upanishad, then Brahmana

questions.q: Which of these conclusions would NOT follow from what the chapter says about the Vedic texts?
questions.a: The Rigveda was first composed in the Ganga plains, far from the Sindhu-Sarasvati region. The chapter says the Rigveda was composed in the northwestern part of the subcontinent, in the Sapta-Sindhu region, not in the Ganga plains.
o: The Rigveda was first composed in the Ganga plains, far from the Sindhu-Sarasvati region
The Rigveda belongs to the northwest, where the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation flourished
The Vedic texts were passed on orally for several centuries before being written
Historians use the Vedic texts to learn about social structures and political systems

questions.q:
Read the statements about society, State and Vedic literature.
1. Society is regulated mainly by formal laws, while customs matter only for a State.
2. The Rigveda is the earliest veda and has 1,028 hymns (suktas).
3. The chanting tradition of the Samaveda forms an important foundation for the system of the seven svaras of Indian music.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 is false: the chapter says society is regulated primarily by customs and practices rather than formal laws. Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Historians can say that the earliest sections of the Rigveda were composed in the northwestern part of the subcontinent.
Reason (R): Both the Rigveda and the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation were familiar with copper.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true. The chapter says the Rigveda was composed where the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation flourished and that both knew copper, but knowing copper does not tell us where the hymns were composed.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A sage-led study group reads the part of a Veda whose name comes from the Sanskrit word for forest because it expands on the philosophical speculations of sages living there. That part is the ___.
questions.a: Aranyaka

questions.q:
Match each Veda with what the chapter says about it.
1. Rigveda
2. Samaveda
3. Atharvaveda
4. Yajurveda
a. Hymns arranged for musical recitation
b. Hymns, some to ward off evil and some about treating physical and mental ailments
c. The earliest veda, with 1,028 hymns
d. Elaborates how yajnas are performed, with explanations in prose
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d. The Rigveda is the earliest with 1,028 hymns; the Samaveda is for musical recitation; the Atharvaveda covers hymns against evil and for treating ailments; the Yajurveda elaborates the performance of yajnas.

questions.q: True or False: Historians agree that the Rigveda was composed in the second millennium BCE. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the date of composition remains debated, with estimates ranging from the fifth millennium BCE to the second millennium BCE.
s: Correction: the date is debated, with estimates from the fifth to the second millennium BCE

questions.q: (a) Name two things that, according to the chapter, a State includes. (b) In a family, nobody is fined for removing shoes at the door, yet everyone does it. Using (a), explain why this is a matter of society and not of the State.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: well-defined rights and duties of rulers and subjects, mechanisms of governance, institutions for enforcing law and order. (b) There is no rule backed by an enforcing institution; the habit is kept up by custom, and the chapter says society is regulated primarily by customs and practices.
s: (a) Two features of a State from the chapter
(b) Custom without an enforcing institution, so society

questions.q: (a) Name the four parts found in each text of a Veda. (b) Which of those parts would a historian open to understand what ritual a household performed, and which to understand the sages' ideas about the Self? Say why.
questions.a: (a) Samhita, Brahmana, Aranyaka and Upanishad. (b) The Brahmana for ritual, since they explain ritual performances; the Upanishads for the Self (Atman) and the Ultimate Universal Being (Brahman).
s: (b) Brahmana for ritual, Upanishad for the Self, with the reason

questions.q: A textbook note says: 'Brahman is a concept, Brahmanas are texts, and Brahmanas/Brahmins is a varna category.' Distinguish the first two, and say what the third refers to.
questions.a: Brahman is the concept of the Ultimate Universal Being; the Brahmanas are texts, composed in prose, that explain ritual performances. Brahmins/Brahmanas as a varna category are a social group, not a text or an idea.
s: Third term identified as a varna category

questions.q: A historian wants to know how people of the Vedic age earned a living and how they worshipped. Why can she use the Vedic literature, and in what form did it exist for several centuries before it was written down?
questions.a: The chapter says Vedic texts give insights into economic pursuits and religious practices, among other things, and the literature existed in oral form for several centuries before being written down.
s: Vedic texts give insights into economic pursuits and religious practices
It existed in oral form for centuries before writing

questions.q: Ravi says: 'The Rigveda was composed in the very region where the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation flourished, so we can fix its date exactly to that civilisation's time.' How far is he right?
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter does place the Rigveda in the northwest, where the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation flourished. But it says the date of composition is debated, with estimates from the fifth to the second millennium BCE, so an exact date cannot be fixed.
s: The right part: the region matches
The wrong part: the date is debated, with the range of estimates

questions.q: A museum plans a wall labelled 'Inside a Veda'. Write a one-line caption for each of the four parts of a Veda text, so that a visitor can tell them apart.
questions.a: Samhita: hymns used to invoke deities and offer oblations in the yajna. Brahmana: prose that explains how rituals are performed. Aranyaka: philosophical speculations of sages living in forests. Upanishad: the Self (Atman) and the Ultimate Universal Being (Brahman).

questions.q: The chapter says society is regulated primarily by customs and a State by rules and laws. Give one everyday example of each, and say why the chapter says States developed only gradually.
questions.a: Example of society: a community eating together at a festival by custom. Example of State: a traffic law enforced by police. The chapter says political systems developed gradually as societies became larger and more complex.
s: A rule-and-enforcement example for the State
Gradual development as societies grew larger and more complex

questions.q: 'The Vedic texts are foundational to Indian culture and traditions.' Justify this statement using the chapter. Refer to what they tell historians, the region of the Rigveda, the four parts of a Veda text and the continuity of practices.
questions.a: They are the earliest known corpus of Indian literature, giving insights into lives, social structures, political systems, economic pursuits and religious practices. The earliest sections of the Rigveda come from Sapta-Sindhu. Each Veda has four parts, from hymns to philosophy. Cultural practices continue (sun worship at Chhath and Makar Sankranti), and the chanting tradition of the Samaveda is a foundation of the seven svaras. So later culture grew on this base.
s: The region and earliness of the Rigveda
The four parts and what each does
Continuity of practices from the chapter
A concluding judgement that links them

questions.q: Compare society and State as the chapter describes them. Then analyse why an early community that became larger and more complex needed the second to develop alongside the first.
questions.a: Society: a system of social relationships among people sharing territory, culture and belonging, with structural units such as families and institutions such as marriage, regulated mainly by custom. State: an organised political system with rules and laws, rights and duties of rulers and subjects, governance and enforcement. Customs alone cannot settle disputes in a large, complex group, so rules and enforcing institutions developed gradually. The chapter notes these systems developed as societies became larger and more complex.
s: The contrast in how each is regulated
Why larger and more complex societies needed a State
Linked to the gradual development noted in the chapter

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur plans an exhibition called 'Voices of the Rigveda'. One exhibit is a hymn-count chart. A second points to a region marked by the Indus, its five tributaries and the Sarasvati. A third says the hymns were chanted for generations before they were written. The hall has room for one more corner: either a recitation corner or a display of written manuscripts.
(a) What name does the chapter give the region, and in what part of the subcontinent is it?
(b) If the Rigveda's hymns are shared equally among 4 reciters, how many does each recite?
(c) A visitor asks whether the hymns were written from the start. Answer using the chapter.
(d) Which corner should the school choose? Give one reason for each choice and then decide.
questions.a: (a) Sapta-Sindhu, in the northwestern part of the subcontinent. (b) 1,028 / 4 = 257 hymns each. (c) No: they existed in oral form for several centuries before being written down. (d) Either may be justified. A recitation corner matches how the hymns lived for centuries; a manuscript display shows how they were preserved in writing later. A sound answer chooses one, uses (c) and admits what the other would show.
s: (c) Oral for several centuries before writing
(d) A trade-off between the two corners, with a justified choice

questions.q:
Meera's history club must write a note on life in India around 1500 BCE. It has two sources: seals carrying Harappan script, and a Vedic text recited aloud. A member suggests the note should say, 'The Rigveda was composed in 1500 BCE exactly, and it alone proves everything about that age.'
(a) What does the chapter say about the Harappan script, and what does that mean for the club's use of the seals' writing?
(b) Name two kinds of information that historians seek from Vedic texts.
(c) Correct the member's sentence using the chapter.
(d) The club can either rely on the Vedic text alone or combine it with archaeological evidence. Which is better? Give one point for each side, then decide.
questions.a: (a) The script has not been deciphered, so its writing cannot be read as evidence. (b) Any two of: times and geographies, lives of people, social structures, political systems, economic pursuits, religious practices. (c) The Rigveda's date is debated, from the fifth to the second millennium BCE, so no exact year can be given, and one text alone cannot prove everything. (d) The text gives ideas, institutions and practices that objects cannot; archaeology gives material evidence that supplements literary sources. A balanced choice, justified, earns the mark.
s: (a) Script undeciphered, so its writing cannot serve as evidence
(c) Date debated, one source cannot prove everything
(d) A justified choice that weighs both sources

questions.q: A museum label shows iron ploughshares, a glossy black deluxe pottery and charred paddy grains from a site near Prayagraj, dated to the second half of the first millennium BCE. What does the chapter say such finds point to in the middle Ganga region?
questions.a: A richer, more advanced material culture with growing agriculture. The chapter links iron implements, a wider variety of grain, paddy and the deluxe NBPW ware to a richer, more advanced material culture in the middle Ganga region.
o: A richer, more advanced material culture with growing agriculture
A fall in the number of settlements as people returned to pastoral clan life
A decline of iron use as stone tools replaced it
The first appearance of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation there

questions.q: In a Vedic gathering, a small body of select elites hears a dispute between two families and gives a ruling. Which of the three assemblies named in the chapter does this most resemble?
questions.a: Sabha, a smaller body that served a judicial function. The chapter describes the sabha as a smaller body of select elites that primarily served a judicial function.
o: Sabha, a smaller body that served a judicial function
Samiti, a larger assembly focused on policy and political affairs
Vidhata, a popular gathering for discussing warfare
Janapada, the territory where a people first set its feet

questions.q: Which statement best describes the change that the word janapada marks, as explained in the chapter?
questions.a: People's identity moved from kinship ties alone towards belonging to a land. Janapada means where a people (jana) first set its feet; the transition between about 1000 and 600 BCE meant identity based on territory as well as kinship.
o: People's identity moved from kinship ties alone towards belonging to a land
People's identity moved from belonging to a land towards kinship ties alone
The rule of a raja was replaced by assemblies of elected members
The mahajanapadas were broken up into smaller clans (janas)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT given in the chapter as a reason for Magadha's rise to power among the mahajanapadas?
questions.a: Its capital lay at the mouth of the Sindhu on the Arabian Sea. The chapter gives strategic location, fertile plains and strong rulers. Magadha was in present-day Bihar, not at the mouth of the Sindhu.
o: Its capital lay at the mouth of the Sindhu on the Arabian Sea
Its strategic location in present-day Bihar
The fertile plains that it controlled
The strong rulers who expanded its control over neighbouring regions

questions.q: On a heritage tour in Tamil Nadu a guide says, 'The bow was the emblem of the Cholas and the tiger of the Pandyas.' A well-read student corrects her. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The tiger was the Chola emblem, the bow the Chera and the fish the Pandya. The chapter says the tiger was the emblem of the Cholas, the bow represented the Cheras and the fish symbolised the Pandyas.
o: The tiger was the Chola emblem, the bow the Chera and the fish the Pandya
The fish was the Chola emblem, the tiger the Chera and the bow the Pandya
The tiger was the Chera emblem, the bow the Chola and the fish the Pandya
The bow was the Pandya emblem, the fish the Chera and the tiger the Chola

questions.q:
Read the statements about early political institutions.
1. The Rigveda alone mentions about thirty janas, five of which formed the panchajana.
2. The janapada stage came after the mahajanapadas, which were smaller units than janapadas.
3. Northern India had both monarchical states (rajyas) and republican states (ganas or samghas).
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says mahajanapadas were bigger political units than janapadas and came later. Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Magadha gradually emerged as the most powerful of the sixteen mahajanapadas.
Reason (R): Its strategic location, fertile plains and strong rulers enabled it to expand its control over neighbouring regions.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and the chapter itself gives the three factors in R as how Magadha expanded and so became the most powerful.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: The Rigveda alone mentions about thirty janas, of which five formed the panchajana. The number of janas outside the panchajana is about ___.
(a) What does janapada literally mean? (b) Using that meaning, explain what changed in people's sense of identity, and between which approximate years the change occurred.
questions.a: (a) Where a people (jana) first set its feet. (b) Identity moved from kinship alone to include belonging to a land, between about 1000 BCE and 600 BCE, so control over land, agriculture and trade routes grew in importance.
s: (b) The shift from kinship to territory, with the years 1000 to 600 BCE

questions.q: (a) Which Vedic assembly was the larger one focused on policy decisions and political affairs, and which the smaller one that served a judicial function? (b) A clan decision on a policy affecting every family had to be taken. Which of the two would suit it better, and why?
questions.a: (a) Samiti was the larger assembly for policy; sabha was the smaller judicial body. (b) The samiti, because it was focused on policy decisions and represented the broader population, while the sabha was composed of select elites.
s: (a) Samiti for policy, sabha for judicial matters
(b) Samiti, with the reason from its size and representation

questions.q: The chapter warns that the early Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms should not be confused with the later imperial kingdoms. What does it say about the later ones, and which literature tells us of the early ones?
questions.a: The later imperial kingdoms emerged many centuries later. Much of what we know about the early ones comes from Sangam literature, composed between 300 BCE and 300 CE.
s: The later imperial kingdoms came many centuries later
Sangam literature (300 BCE-300 CE) is the source for the early ones

questions.q: What were rajyas and what were ganas or samghas? Say what their existence together shows about northern India around 600 BCE.
questions.a: Rajyas were monarchical states and ganas or samghas were republican states. Their coexistence shows that northern India had different forms of political organisation.
s: Rajyas as monarchical, ganas/samghas as republican
Different forms of political organisation existed together

questions.q: After the shift from janas to janapadas, give two reasons from the chapter why more complex administrative systems became necessary.
questions.a: Control over land, agricultural production and trade routes became increasingly important, which led to more complex administrative systems.
s: Control over land and agricultural production became important
Control over trade routes became important

questions.q: Kabir says: 'In the Vedic period the raja decided everything alone; there was nothing beside him.' Test this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the raja functioned mainly as a clan chief who led in warfare and protected members, and it names three assemblies (sabha, samiti, vidhata) that played a significant role in early Vedic polity. The claim ignores these.
s: The raja's role as clan chief for war and protection
The three assemblies that also had a role

questions.q: Show in three steps how Vedic kin-based clans grew into the mahajanapadas, giving the approximate period of each of the last two steps.
questions.a: Janas (clans) led by a raja; then janapadas, territorial units, about 1000 to 600 BCE; then mahajanapadas, bigger political units, about 600 BCE to 300 CE.
s: Mahajanapada with its period (about 600 BCE-300 CE)

questions.q: Give three pieces of evidence that the chapter uses to show that the Ganga region was changing in the first millennium BCE.
questions.a: Any three of: more settlements concentrated in the Ganga region, increasing use of iron implements, a wider variety of grain, characteristic PGW pottery, deluxe ware NBPW, expanding agriculture and greater paddy cultivation.

questions.q: Describe how political organisation changed from the kin-based polities of the Rigveda to the sixteen mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha, bringing in the part played by the Ganga region.
questions.a: Early Vedic society was organised into janas led by a raja, with assemblies. Between about 1000 and 600 BCE territory became the basis of identity (janapadas). From about 600 BCE bigger mahajanapadas arose, sixteen in the sources. The Ganga plains became the main centre as agriculture, iron and richer material culture grew. Magadha, in present-day Bihar, expanded and led to the Mauryan Empire.
s: Janapadas and the shift to territory
The Ganga region's growth in agriculture and material culture
Magadha's rise leading to the Mauryan Empire

questions.q: Compare the political units of northern and southern India between 600 BCE and 300 CE as the chapter describes them, and justify why the southern polities should not be thought of as a copy of the north.
questions.a: North: monarchical rajyas and republican ganas or samghas, with the Mauryan Empire succeeded in the Deccan by the Satavahana Empire (nearly 500 years). South: polities of the Cholas (lower Kaveri), Pandyas (Tamraparni and Vaigai), Keralaputras or Cheras (Kerala) and Satiyaputras (northern Tamil Nadu), mentioned in Ashokan inscriptions, with their own emblems and the Sangam literature of 300 BCE to 300 CE. They had their own rice-growing regions, crowned kings and traditions, so they were not copies.
s: The Satavahana Empire in the Deccan
The southern polities and where each lay
Emblems and Sangam literature as their own tradition

questions.q:
A district museum in Nalanda shows three finds from the Ganga region: an iron sickle, a glossy black bowl and a bag of paddy. The curator's label says: 'Evidence of a growing region that gave rise to the most powerful of the sixteen mahajanapadas.' The museum can spend its remaining budget either on a large map of the mahajanapadas or on replicas of the iron tools and pottery.
(a) Which mahajanapada does the label point to, and in which present-day state was it?
(b) What is the glossy black ware called in the chapter?
(c) Give two reasons from the chapter why this mahajanapada could expand.
(d) Which spending would better tell the story of its rise? Give one point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Magadha, in present-day Bihar. (b) NBPW (Northern Black Polished Ware), the deluxe ware. (c) Strategic location, fertile plains and strong rulers. (d) A map shows the strategic location and neighbours; replicas show the iron and farming base. A reasoned choice that uses (c) earns the mark.
s: (d) A justified choice between map and replicas

questions.q:
A group planning a heritage walk in Tamil Nadu has three flags: a tiger, a bow and a fish. The guide's notes say that Sangam poems tell of a Chera ruler who earned a title after defeating several crowned kings, and that the Ashokan inscriptions also mention southern polities. Time allows either a reading from Sangam poems or a display on the Ashokan inscriptions.
(a) Name the kingdom of each flag.
(b) Between which years was Sangam literature composed, and what does the chapter call the three rulers together?
(c) A participant says the walk will show the imperial Cholas of the 9th-11th centuries CE through these poems. Correct her.
(d) Which display would give a better picture of the southern polities? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Tiger: Cholas; bow: Cheras; fish: Pandyas. (b) 300 BCE to 300 CE; the three crowned kings or Vendar of Tamilakam. (c) Sangam literature describes the early kingdoms, which should not be confused with the later imperial kingdoms that emerged many centuries later. (d) Sangam poems give detail on kings and fertile rice regions; Ashokan inscriptions confirm Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras and Satiyaputras as polities. Either, with a reason.
s: (b) 300 BCE-300 CE and the three crowned kings
(c) Early kingdoms are not the later imperial ones
(d) A justified choice between poems and inscriptions

questions.q: At a coronation, a priest recalls the oath of the Yajurveda as the chapter reports it. Which of these would he NOT include in the king's pledge?
questions.a: To favour the strong over the weak. The chapter reports the oath as judging the strong and weak impartially and fairly, protecting the country from calamities and doing good to the people; favouring the strong would contradict the first.
o: To favour the strong over the weak
To judge the strong and the weak impartially and fairly
To protect the country from all calamities
To do good to the people

questions.q: Invaders capture a kingdom's fortified towns and empty its treasury, though the king, ministers, army, territory and allies survive. Which two constituents of Kautilya's saptanga are directly lost?
questions.a: Durga (forts) and kosha (treasury). Durga is the fortified towns and cities, and kosha is the treasury or wealth of the kingdom.
o: Durga (forts) and kosha (treasury)
Danda (the forces) and mitra (the allies)
Amatya (the ministers) and janapada (the territory)
Swami (the king) and mitra (the allies)

questions.q: A student says, 'Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda, so the Cholas wanted to rule only the Ganga region.' What does the chapter use this example to show?
questions.a: The repeated aim of ruling the whole subcontinent. The title was adopted to commemorate his conquest of regions along the Ganga, and the chapter says it is one more expression of the aspiration to political authority over the subcontinent.
o: The repeated aim of ruling the whole subcontinent
That the Cholas ruled the Ganga plains for the whole 11th century
That the idea of chakravarti kshetra ended after the Mauryas
That Rajendra I rejected the Arthashastra's idea of prithivi

questions.q: Ashoka's edict says his 'energetic exertions' led to 'significant changes in the spiritual life in Jambudvipa'. What does the chapter say about the way such a term was used?
questions.a: It shows an awareness reaching beyond his kingdom. The chapter says the pan-Indian awareness of early monarchs went beyond their kingdoms' boundaries and was expressed through terms such as Jambudvipa and Bharatavarsha.
o: It shows an awareness reaching beyond his kingdom
It shows he ruled only the region around his capital
It shows he gave up the claims of kingship for a life of renunciation
It shows that Jambudvipa meant the sea that bounded the kingdom

questions.q:
Read the statements about kingship and the state.
1. The Arthashastra lists seven constituents of the state, which can function effectively only if they remain properly integrated.
2. The council of ministers was a large body of young warriors whose only role was to command the army.
3. An Ashokan inscription shows that the council of ministers could never take a decision while the emperor was away.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only. Statements 2 and 3 are false: the council was a small body of elder statesmen who advised the king, and an Ashokan inscription refers to decisions it took during the emperor's absence. Statement 1 is from the chapter.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Arthashastra treats the state as an organic whole made of seven constituents.
Reason (R): The seven constituents it names are the king, his queens, the priests, the forts, the treasury, the army and the allies.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. A is true. R is false: the seven constituents are the king, the ministers, the territory, the forts, the treasury, the army and the allies; queens and priests are not among them.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each ruler with the record or title the chapter connects to him.
1. Ashoka
2. Rudradaman I
3. Skandagupta
4. Rajendra I
a. A long Sanskrit inscription on his military achievements and the repair of the Sudarshana Lake
b. Major Rock Edicts in Prakrit spreading the message of Dhamma
c. A record noting the restoration of the lake after severe damage
d. The title Gangaikonda for conquests along the Ganga
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. Ashoka's edicts are in Prakrit and spread Dhamma; Rudradaman I's long Sanskrit inscription covers conquests and the lake's repair; Skandagupta recorded restoration after damage; Rajendra I took Gangaikonda.

questions.q: A kingdom has lost its forts and its treasury but keeps the other constituents of Kautilya's saptanga. The number of the seven constituents that remain is ___.

(a) Name any three officers the council of ministers (mantri-parishad) generally included. (b) Why does an Ashokan inscription about decisions in the emperor's absence matter when judging the council's powers?
questions.a: (a) Any three of: the treasurer, the chief tax collector, the chief legal advisor, the commander-in-chief of the army. (b) It shows that in exceptional circumstances the council could take decisions independently, in public interest.
s: (b) The council could decide independently in exceptional circumstances

questions.q: (a) What idea does the Arthashastra's statement 'one wheel does not move the carriage' capture? (b) A king dismisses all his councillors and ministers. Name the saptanga constituent he has lost and say what the chapter says about such a state.
questions.a: (a) Effective governance needs cooperation and a well-organised administrative machinery. (b) Amatya (councillors, ministers and high officials); the state can function effectively only if its constituents remain properly integrated.
s: (b) Amatya lost, and a state needs its constituents integrated

questions.q: The chapter says kingship was generally hereditary, yet there are references to kings being elected or even expelled. What does this suggest about royal authority and about succession?
questions.a: It suggests that royal authority was not always absolute and that succession was not entirely hereditary in practice.
s: Royal authority was not always absolute
Succession was not entirely hereditary in practice

questions.q: The Junagadh Rock Inscription carries records of three rulers over about 700 years. Give two kinds of information the chapter says it provides.
questions.a: It provides valuable information about administration, public works and political history in India (any two).

questions.q: The Shanti Parva of the Mahabharata guides rulers. State two responsibilities of the king that the chapter draws from it, and name one offence he was expected to judge.
questions.a: He was to protect subjects from external threats and from internal disorder, and to administer justice in cases such as abduction, robbery, theft or adultery.
s: Two responsibilities: protection from threats and disorder, and justice

questions.q: Tara says: 'The wish to rule the whole subcontinent is not a single king's idea; it comes up again and again, from Ashoka's edict to a Sangam Chera king to the Cholas.' Test her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Ashoka's edict speaks of Jambudvipa; the Chera king Nedunjeral Adan won the rank of adhiraja and extended conquests to the Himalayas; Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda. The chapter says the aspiration was repeatedly expressed.
s: Ashoka and the Chera king as evidence
Rajendra I and the chapter's conclusion of repeated expression

questions.q: A ruler has a king, ministers, an army and allies. Using Kautilya's list, show that this is not a complete state and name what is missing.
questions.a: Four of the seven constituents are present (swami, amatya, danda, mitra). Missing are the territory with its population (janapada), the forts (durga) and the treasury (kosha). The state can function effectively only if all seven are integrated.
s: All seven must be integrated for effective functioning

questions.q: Texts like the Mahabharata and the Arthashastra describe protecting people and ensuring justice as the king's duty. Explain in three points what this suggests about the relationship between ruler and subjects.
questions.a: The king was expected to protect his subjects from external threats and internal disorder; he was to administer justice; his authority was not absolute, since kings could be elected or expelled. So the relationship rested on duty to the people, not unlimited power.
s: Authority not absolute, so ruler accountable

questions.q: 'The aspiration to exercise political authority over the Indian subcontinent was repeatedly expressed in the history of Indian kingship.' Justify with examples from the chapter.
questions.a: Terms such as Jambudvipa, Bharatavarsha, Ashvamedha and Rajasuya yajna, Prithivi and chakravarti kshetra carried the idea. Ashoka's edict speaks of Jambudvipa. The Arthashastra defines prithivi as the area between the Himavat and the sea, equating it with chakravarti kshetra. The Chera king Nedunjeral Adan extended conquests to the Himalayas. Rajendra I took the title Gangaikonda in the 11th century CE. Examples from the Mauryan, Sangam and Chola periods show the idea recurring.
s: The terms that expressed the idea
Prithivi and chakravarti kshetra in the Arthashastra
A conclusion about repetition across periods

questions.q: Analyse how the saptanga, the council of ministers and the king's duties together describe a state in which the king did not rule alone.
questions.a: Kautilya's seven constituents make the king only one part of the state, and the state works only when all are integrated. 'One wheel does not move the carriage' says governance needs cooperation. The mantri-parishad of elder statesmen advised the king and included the treasurer, chief tax collector, chief legal advisor and commander-in-chief. An Ashokan inscription shows it could decide in the emperor's absence. The king's duties of protection and justice were to be carried out through such machinery.
s: The king as one of seven constituents
'One wheel' and the need for cooperation
The Ashokan inscription showing independent decisions
A conclusion linking duties to the machinery

questions.q:
A class from Ahmedabad visits Girnar, where one rock carries the records of three rulers from different periods, spanning about 700 years. The guide says one record is a long Sanskrit inscription and another is in Prakrit. The class has funds for either a rubbing exhibition of the three records or a model of the Sudarshana Lake.
(a) Name the three rulers whose records the rock holds, in time order.
(b) What does the long Sanskrit inscription describe?
(c) The last record concerns the lake. What does it note?
(d) Which spending better shows what the rock teaches about administration and public works? Give one point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta. (b) His military achievements and the repair of the Sudarshana Lake. (c) The restoration of the lake after severe damage. (d) The rubbings show three rulers and languages over 700 years; the model shows the public work itself. A reasoned choice that uses (b) and (c) earns the mark.
s: (b) Military achievements and repair of the lake
(d) A justified choice between rubbings and model

questions.q:
King Veer of a small realm has a strong army and a full treasury, but he has appointed few ministers and his forts are in disrepair. His advisers disagree: one wants the next year's revenue spent on repairing forts, the other on appointing more ministers and winning allies.
(a) In Kautilya's terms, name the two constituents in which the king is weak.
(b) What does the Arthashastra's wheel statement say about governance, and how does it apply here?
(c) Name two officers who would normally sit in a council of ministers.
(d) Which spending would you advise? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Amatya (ministers) and durga (forts). (b) One wheel does not move the carriage: governance needs cooperation and an organised machinery, so a king who relies on army and treasury alone is weak. (c) Any two of the treasurer, chief tax collector, chief legal advisor, commander-in-chief. (d) Forts guard against external threat; ministers and allies run the state and advise. Either with a reason that keeps the constituents integrated.
s: (b) The wheel statement applied to the king
(d) A justified choice that weighs both spendings

questions.q: A record from 400 CE refers to a 'bhukti' governed from a northern capital, while a record of the same period from Tamil country mentions a 'mandalam'. What does the chapter say about the two?
questions.a: Both are provinces: bhukti in the north, mandalam in the south. The chapter says that between about 300 and 800 CE kingdoms were divided into provinces, known as bhuktis in the north and mandalas or mandalams in the south.
o: Both are provinces: bhukti in the north, mandalam in the south
Both are villages: bhukti in the north, mandalam in the south
A bhukti is a district and a mandalam a group of villages
A bhukti is a city governor's office and a mandalam a village assembly

questions.q: A Gupta-period record names a new officer who advised the emperor on treaties and on declaring war. Which post does the chapter say was introduced for this?
questions.a: Sandhivigrahika, the minister of peace and war. The chapter says a new minister of peace and war, the sandhivigrahika, was introduced under the Guptas, while the mantri remained head of civil administration.
o: Sandhivigrahika, the minister of peace and war
Mantri, the head of the civil administration
Kumaramatya, an administrator at the local or provincial level
Pradeshika, a district governor with judicial functions

questions.q: A historian finds that a Pallava village repaired its tank through a committee of its own assembly, without waiting for a royal order. Which feature from the chapter does this best illustrate?
questions.a: Assemblies ran tasks through committees (variyams). The chapter says village assemblies had small committees, variyams, that managed tasks such as irrigation, gardens and temple management.
o: Assemblies ran tasks through committees (variyams)
The Pallavas had given up monarchy for republican rule
Village headmen (gramikas) were chosen by the committee
Tax-free Brahmadeya grants removed the need for any assembly

questions.q: Which of these statements about administration between 300 and 800 CE is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Power was fully centralised, so provinces had no officers of their own. The period is described as one of decentralisation of power, with a large machinery of provincial governors and district officers.
o: Power was fully centralised, so provinces had no officers of their own
The kingdom was divided into provinces, divisions and districts
The village was the lowest administrative unit
The king was supreme, with officers working at provincial and local levels

questions.q:
Read the statements about village and district administration.
1. The Damodarpur copper plates of Kumaragupta I record a district office of five members.
2. Under the Cholas, village assemblies depended on royal patronage for their local work.
3. Candidates for village assembly elections at Uttaramerur were required to have honest earnings and a pure mind.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says Chola village assemblies functioned as independent, self-reliant institutions, not dependent on the government for patronage. Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under the Cholas, village assemblies could collect revenue and manage irrigation only after receiving orders from the royal court.
Reason (R): Chola village assemblies were responsible for local administrative functions, including revenue collection, land management and irrigation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. A is false: the chapter says village assemblies were self-reliant and not dependent on the government for patronage. R is true; it is the reason A cannot hold.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
Match each northern term with its southern counterpart in the chapter's account of administrative units.
1. Bhukti (province)
2. Vishaya or bhoga (division)
3. Adhishthana or pattana (district)
4. Vithi (group of villages)
a. Nadu
b. Kottam or valanadu
c. Mandalam
d. Pattala or kurram
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-a, 4-d. Province: bhukti and mandalam; division: vishaya/bhoga and kottam/valanadu; district: adhishthana/pattana and nadu; group of villages: vithi and pattala/kurram.

questions.q: The Pallava dynasty is dated c. 275-897 CE and the Chalukyas of Badami c. 543-753 CE. The Pallavas lasted ___ years longer than the Chalukyas.
True or False: In the Chola empire, village assemblies handled local work such as revenue collection, irrigation and road construction on their own. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says village assemblies were responsible for all local administrative functions, including revenue collection, land management, irrigation, road construction and record maintenance, and functioned as independent, self-reliant institutions.
s: Reason: the assemblies handled these functions and did not depend on the government for patronage

questions.q: (a) What were the provinces called in the north and in the south between 300 and 800 CE? (b) Why does the chapter describe this as a period of decentralisation?
questions.a: (a) Bhuktis in the north and mandalas or mandalams in the south. (b) For administrative convenience the kingdom (rajya) was divided into several provinces, subdivided into divisions, districts and villages, so power was spread among officers at different levels.
s: (b) Kingdom divided into several levels for administrative convenience

questions.q: (a) Name the five members of the district office recorded in the Damodarpur copper plates. (b) Three of them came from trade and craft, not from the royal service. Which three, and what does that suggest about how a district was run?
questions.a: (a) The head district officer, the chief banker, the chief caravan trader, the chief artisan and the chief of revenue collection. (b) The banker, caravan trader and artisan; district decisions involved important local residents, not only royal officers.
s: (b) Banker, caravan trader, artisan, and the involvement of local residents

questions.q: Distinguish between the Brahmadeya villages of the Pallavas and the agraharams of the Chalukyas, and say what some agraharams became.
questions.a: Brahmadeya villages were villages given tax-free land grants by the Pallavas; agraharams were Brahmin settlements given land grants by the Chalukyas. Some, such as those at Aihole and Badami, developed into prominent centres of learning.
s: Some agraharams grew into centres of learning

questions.q: Name the new post the Guptas added to Kautilya's scheme, and say who the kumaramatyas were.
questions.a: The new post was the sandhivigrahika, a minister of peace and war. Kumaramatyas were administrators at the local or provincial level, a broader category into which the earlier amatyas evolved.
s: Sandhivigrahika, minister of peace and war
Kumaramatyas as administrators at local or provincial level

questions.q: Name the three powers in the 'tri-partite struggle' for Kannauj, and say what the administration of all three had in common.
questions.a: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas. All followed a mix of monarchy and decentralised units of provinces, districts and villages, with the village the smallest and largely self-reliant unit.
s: The common pattern: monarchy with decentralised units

questions.q: Harsh says: 'In early empires everything, from irrigation to justice, was decided at the capital; villages had no say.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says villages functioned relatively independently of royal administration. Pallava village assemblies had variyams for irrigation, gardens and temples, and Chola village assemblies handled revenue, land, irrigation and roads. The village was the smallest unit and largely self-reliant in several empires.
s: Chola village assemblies' functions as evidence

questions.q: A school wants to choose its council by the Kudavolai method. Write the three main steps, each tied to the Uttaramerur account.
questions.a: Names of eligible candidates are written on palm leaves and placed in a large pot. During a public gathering a young child draws the leaves one by one, in full view of the community. The elected members are then divided into specialised committees (variyams).
s: Names on palm leaves in a pot
A young child draws them in public

questions.q: Compare Gupta administration with Kautilya's scheme: say what was retained, what was new and what had changed.
questions.a: Retained: the mantri as head of the civil administration, with a commander-in-chief, a general and the chief of the palace guards. New: the minister of peace and war (sandhivigrahika). Changed: the amatyas evolved into a broader category including kumaramatyas.

questions.q: Describe the levels of administration in the north and south between 300 and 800 CE and explain how the king's supreme authority was combined with decentralised local government.
questions.a: The kingdom (rajya) was divided into provinces (bhuktis in the north, mandalams in the south), then divisions (vishaya or bhoga; kottams or valanadu), districts (adhishthana or pattana; nadu), groups of villages (vithis; pattala and kurram) and finally villages. The king was supreme, but officers at provincial and local levels did the general administration. Pradeshikas handled judicial and administrative tasks after consulting local residents. Villages ran irrigation, justice and taxation through assemblies and committees. So central authority and local self-rule were combined.
s: The king's supreme authority and officers at each level
Consultation of local residents by district officers

questions.q: 'The village assemblies of the Chola empire functioned as independent, self-reliant institutions.' Justify, using the Uttaramerur inscription and the functions of the assemblies.
questions.a: The Chola empire was divided into mandalams, valanadus, nadus and urs, with the village the smallest unit. Village assemblies settled disputes and were responsible for revenue collection, land management, irrigation, road construction and records, and were not dependent on the government for patronage. The Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I describes the Kudavolai system, in which names on palm leaves were drawn by a young child in public, and members were divided into variyams for the tank, justice and taxes. Qualifications such as honest earnings and a pure mind show self-set standards.
s: The position of the village in the Chola structure

questions.q:
A school in Kanchipuram district stages a 'Kudavolai' election for its student council. Forty-five students are eligible. Their names are written on slips and placed in a pot, and a Class 6 student draws them in front of the whole school. Fifteen slips are drawn, and the chosen students are divided equally into three committees. A teacher suggests doing the draw privately in the staff room to save time.
(a) Which inscription describes the original system, and of which ruler and century?
(b) How many students sit on each committee, and how many names remain in the pot?
(c) Name the two qualities the inscription required of candidates.
(d) Should the school follow the original public draw or the staff-room draw? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) The Uttaramerur inscription of Parantaka I, 10th century CE. (b) 15 / 3 = 5 students on each committee; 45 - 15 = 30 names remain. (c) Honest earnings and a pure mind. (d) A private draw saves time, but the original draw was in full view of the community to ensure fairness. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (c) Honest earnings and a pure mind
(d) A justified choice between public and private draw

questions.q:
In a Gupta-period district, a dispute over a land sale reaches the district office. The office has a head officer, a banker, a caravan trader, an artisan and a revenue chief. Local traders complain that consulting so many people slows decisions and suggest that the head officer should decide alone.
(a) How many members does the chapter say the district office had, and which copper plates record it?
(b) Name the kinds of local residents whom district officers often consulted before deciding.
(c) The pradeshikas combined two kinds of function. Name them.
(d) Should the head officer decide alone or keep consulting? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Five members; the Damodarpur copper plates of Kumaragupta I. (b) Bankers, caravan leaders, artisans and scribes. (c) Judicial and administrative functions. (d) Deciding alone is faster; consulting brings local knowledge and the support of important residents, as the chapter describes. Either, if reasoned.
s: (d) A justified choice between speed and consultation

questions.q: A school notice says, 'Dharma means following the rituals of your own religion.' Mr Rao objects, citing the chapter. Which statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: Dharma means duty and moral conduct, not religion. The chapter says that dharma does not mean religion; it refers to duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct, and dhamma is its Pali equivalent.
o: Dharma means duty and moral conduct, not religion
Dharma means religion, while dhamma is a different idea in Buddhism
Dharma means the law enforced by a ruler through punishment
Dharma means the all-pervading cosmic order, which the Rigveda calls samatva

questions.q: A farmer remarks that seasons turn and rivers flow in a steady order and that human society too must keep its balance. Which concept does the chapter use for this all-pervading cosmic order?
questions.a: Rita. The chapter describes rita in the Rigveda as an all-pervading cosmic order that represents harmony and balance in nature and in human society.
o: Rita
Samatva
Dhamma
Satya

questions.q: Which pair correctly links a historical record with the ethical value the chapter connects to it?
questions.a: Ashoka's edicts: non-violence and compassion; Uttaramerur: honest earnings. Ashoka's edicts promoted moral conduct, respect within the family, non-violence and compassion; the 10th-century Uttaramerur inscription required honest earnings and a pure mind of candidates.
o: Ashoka's edicts: non-violence and compassion; Uttaramerur: honest earnings
Ashoka's edicts with honest earnings; the Uttaramerur inscription with non-violence
Ashoka's edicts with the Kudavolai pot; the Uttaramerur inscription with respect in the family
Ashoka's edicts with samatva; the Uttaramerur inscription with the idea of rita

questions.q: Which of these is NOT something the chapter says about the word dharma?
questions.a: It is the Sanskrit word for religion as a set of rituals. The chapter explicitly says dharma does not mean religion; it means duty, righteousness and moral conduct.
o: It is the Sanskrit word for religion as a set of rituals
It is derived from the root dhri, also the root of dharati (the earth)
Bhishma says whatever upholds all beings is dharma
Its Pali equivalent, dhamma, is used in Buddhism for similar ethical principles

questions.q: Shanti reads in the chapter that 'the dharma of iron is to sink and of wood is to float.' What sense of dharma does this example illustrate?
questions.a: The law of existence of each thing. The chapter introduces this saying as dharma in the sense of the law of existence, drawn from the root meaning of what upholds.
o: The law of existence of each thing
A penalty fixed by a king for those who break a rule
The duty of a student towards a teacher
The belief that all things are made of one matter

questions.q:
Read the statements about ethics in early India.
1. Samatva holds that different bodies are made of different matter, so discrimination is natural.
2. The epics critique discrimination and present goodness as non-discriminatory.
3. Ashoka's edicts left out respect within the family from the moral conduct they promoted.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. Statement 1 is false: samatva says all bodies are made of the same matter. Statement 3 is false: Ashoka's edicts emphasised respect within the family. Statement 2 is from the chapter.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter links the word dharma with the earth.
Reason (R): Dharma is derived from the Sanskrit root dhri, which is also the root of dharati (the earth).
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and R explains A: the shared root dhri is why the chapter connects the word dharma with the earth.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A village council adopts the Uttaramerur rule. It would reject a candidate whose earnings are not ___.
questions.a: honest

questions.q: (a) State the principle of samatva as the chapter explains it. (b) How does the chapter say the Mahabharata supports it?
questions.a: (a) All bodies are made of the same matter, and all forms of consciousness are manifestations of one supreme consciousness. (b) The Mahabharata includes characters from all varnas who, despite their differences, repeatedly uphold samatva.
s: (a) Same matter and one supreme consciousness
(b) Characters from all varnas uphold samatva

questions.q: (a) Name the Pali equivalent of the word dharma. (b) Give two ideas that Ashoka's edicts promoted under this banner.
questions.a: (a) Dhamma. (b) Any two of: moral conduct, respect within the family, ethical behaviour in everyday life, non-violence, compassion.

questions.q: Distinguish rita from dharma in one line each, using the chapter.
questions.a: Rita is an all-pervading cosmic order representing harmony and balance in nature and society. Dharma is duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct that individuals are expected to perform according to their roles.
s: Dharma as duty and moral conduct

questions.q: Bhishma says, 'whatever upholds all beings is dharma.' A canteen worker refuses to sell expired food to students. Explain how this act fits the saying.
questions.a: The saying makes dharma whatever upholds beings. Refusing to sell expired food protects the students' wellbeing, so it upholds them and is an act of dharma.
s: The canteen worker's act applied to it

questions.q: Show with two examples that the chapter finds the link between politics and ethics from the Mauryas to the Cholas.
questions.a: Ashoka's edicts (Mauryan) promoted dhamma, with non-violence and compassion; the 10th-century Uttaramerur inscription (Chola period) required honest earnings and a pure mind of candidates.

questions.q: Imran says: 'In the chapter, dharma means religion, so Ashoka's dhamma was only about rituals.' Test the claim.
questions.a: No. The chapter says dharma does not mean religion but duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct, and dhamma is its Pali equivalent. Ashoka's edicts promoted moral conduct, respect within the family, non-violence and compassion, not rituals.
s: Dharma means duty and moral conduct, not religion
Ashoka's edicts promoted conduct and compassion

questions.q: Draft a three-line code of conduct for a village council that uses one idea each from samatva, dharma and the Uttaramerur rule.
questions.a: Example: 1. All villagers are treated alike, since all share the same matter and one consciousness (samatva). 2. Each member does his or her duty with righteousness (dharma). 3. Only people with honest earnings and a pure mind may stand for office (Uttaramerur).
s: A line based on dharma as duty
A line based on the Uttaramerur qualification

questions.q: Explain how the epics, as the chapter describes them, treat discrimination, and what they present as the ideal of a good person and ruler.
questions.a: The epics critique discrimination and present goodness as non-discriminatory; the Mahabharata has characters of all varnas who uphold samatva. They emphasise the ideal of a good person and ruler as one who works for the welfare of all beings.
s: Characters of all varnas uphold samatva
The ideal ruler works for the welfare of all beings

questions.q: Explain, with evidence from the chapter, how ethical ideas guided both state and society from the Vedic texts to the Chola period.
questions.a: The Vedas and epics discuss right conduct, and the Gita emphasises knowledge, faith, action and virtue. Samatva, rita and dharma gave ideas of sameness, order and duty. Ashoka's edicts promoted dhamma in governance. The Uttaramerur inscription required honest earnings and a pure mind of candidates. Works such as Kamandaka's Nitisara and Banabhatta's Kadambari reflect on kingship. So ethics ran through law, rulers and society.
s: Vedas, epics and the Gita on right conduct

questions.q: Compare samatva, rita and dharma as the chapter defines them, and judge which of the three best supports the ideal of a ruler who 'works for the welfare of all beings'.
questions.a: Samatva: all bodies made of the same matter and one supreme consciousness. Rita: an all-pervading cosmic order giving harmony and balance in nature and society. Dharma: duty, obligation, righteousness and moral conduct, what upholds beings. Samatva supports treating all alike; rita supports balance; dharma turns these into duties. A reasoned judgement may choose dharma because it gives the ruler duties toward all, or samatva because it denies discrimination.
s: Link of each to the ruler's ideal

questions.q:
A village council in Tamil Nadu is revising its election rules. The elders propose that candidates should have honest earnings and be pure of mind, as in an old inscription. The youth want to add that candidates should be skilled in accounts. Twelve people have applied, and three are found to have dishonest earnings.
(a) Which record contains the honesty rule, and from which century?
(b) How many candidates remain, and how many on each of three committees if they are shared equally?
(c) Which principle, according to the chapter, ties this rule to ethics?
(d) Should the council keep only the honesty rule or add skill in accounts? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) The Uttaramerur inscription, 10th century CE. (b) 12 - 3 = 9 remain; 9 / 3 = 3 on each committee. (c) The link between politics and ethics, with honest earnings and a pure mind as ethical standards for public life. (d) Honesty protects public trust; skill helps run accounts. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (d) A justified choice between honesty alone and adding skill

questions.q:
A school's Values Week must open with one theme. Group A wants a theme on non-violence and respect for elders, as in Ashoka's edicts. Group B wants a theme of equal treatment of every student, whatever the background, based on a principle that all bodies are made of the same matter.
(a) What is the principle Group B is using called in the chapter?
(b) Name two things that Ashoka's edicts promoted.
(c) What does the chapter say the epics did about discrimination?
(d) Which theme should open the week? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Samatva. (b) Any two of: moral conduct, respect within the family, ethical behaviour in everyday life, non-violence, compassion. (c) They critique discrimination and present goodness as non-discriminatory. (d) Ashoka's themes guide daily conduct; samatva grounds equal treatment. Either with a reason.
s: (d) A justified choice between the two themes

questions.q: Aditi reads the Rigveda verse in which a poet says, 'my father is a physician, my mother a grinder of corn.' What does the chapter draw from it?
questions.a: Occupations in a family could differ, so they were flexible. The chapter uses this verse as evidence of occupational diversity within a single family at a stage when strict hereditary occupations had not yet become firmly established.
o: Occupations in a family could differ, so they were flexible
Women of the Vedic age could follow only one occupation, grinding corn
Every Vedic family was divided into exactly three occupations
The verse proves that varna was a rigid system in the Rigveda

questions.q: The Mandsaur Stone Inscription (473 CE) records a guild of silk weavers that moved from Lata in Gujarat to Dashapura in Madhya Pradesh and became skilled in archery and astrology as well. What does the chapter say this shows?
questions.a: Occupational mobility within social groups. The chapter cites the Mandsaur inscription as an instance of occupational mobility within social groups during the Gupta period.
o: Occupational mobility within social groups
That the guild had lost its original craft
That jati had no connection with occupation
That guilds existed only in the south

questions.q: A community that has migrated to a new region begins to marry only within its own group, and is soon counted as a separate social group. Which factor in the chapter's explanation of the rise of jati does this describe?
questions.a: Migrating communities turning endogamous. The chapter lists intermarriage among varnas, migrating communities becoming endogamous and territorial differences; endogamy means marrying within one's own group.
o: Migrating communities turning endogamous
Intermarriage among the varnas
Territorial differences
The fixed number of four varnas

questions.q: Which of these was NOT among the factors the chapter says shaped social identity in early Vedic texts?
questions.a: A fixed status assigned strictly at birth. The chapter says early Vedic texts do not indicate any fixed social status strictly based on birth; identity was shaped by ethnicity, subgroups, region, village, gotra, language and especially occupation.
o: A fixed status assigned strictly at birth
Occupation
Gotra, a kinship-based subgroup
Geographic region and village affiliation

questions.q: At 58, Mr Nair hands his business to his son and moves to a hut in the forest, keeping only a few belongings. Which of the four ashramas does this match?
questions.a: Vanaprastha, life in the forest. The chapter lists the stages as brahmacharya (studentship), grihastha (householder), vanaprastha (life in the forest) and samnyasa (renunciation).
o: Vanaprastha, life in the forest
Grihastha, the stage of the householder
Brahmacharya, the stage of studentship
Samnyasa, renunciation

questions.q:
Read the statements about the family and society in the Vedic age.
1. The kula was the smallest and most basic social unit, and several families formed a grama.
2. A group of gramas formed a visha headed by a vishapati, and above the visha stood the jana.
3. The chapter lists five ashramas through which every life was divided.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Statement 3 is false: the chapter names four ashramas. Statements 1 and 2 describe the ladder from kula to grama, visha and jana.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The number of jatis kept growing while the number of varnas stayed at four.
Reason (R): The earliest reference to the four social categories is in the Purushasukta, a hymn in Book 10 of the Rigveda.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true. The chapter says there was no restriction on the number of jatis as new groups and occupations developed, but the date and place of the earliest reference to varna does not explain why jatis multiplied.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each varna with the role the chapter associates with it.
1. Brahmanas
2. Rajanya (Kshatriyas)
3. Vaishyas
4. Shudras
a. Warfare, protecting people and administering justice
b. Studying and teaching the Vedas, officiating yajnas, giving and receiving dana
c. Assisting the other varnas, though in practice also farming, trade and crafts
d. Agriculture, pastoralism and trade
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c. Brahmanas studied, taught and officiated; Rajanya fought, protected and gave justice; Vaishyas farmed, herded and traded; Shudras assisted the others and, in practice, also worked in farming, trade and crafts.

questions.q: A trader earns a large profit and spends part of it on a village well. The chapter says artha is desirable if it is guided by ___.
questions.a: dharma

questions.q: True or False: The number of jatis, like the number of varnas, was fixed. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The number of varnas was fixed at four, but there was no restriction on the number of jatis, which continued to grow as new social groups and occupations developed.
s: Correction: varnas fixed at four, jatis unrestricted and growing

questions.q: (a) Name the four purusharthas. (b) Which two does the chapter call particularly significant ethically, and how must the pursuit of artha be guided?
questions.a: (a) Dharma, artha, kama and moksha. (b) Dharma and moksha; artha should be guided by dharma, that is, aligned with the welfare of society.
s: (b) Dharma and moksha; artha guided by dharma

questions.q: (a) According to the Buddhist text Sutta Nipata quoted in the chapter, what makes a person a brahmana? (b) How does this support the chapter's claim that varna was a functional division?
questions.a: (a) Deeds, not birth: 'No brahmana is such by birth ... a brahmana is such by his deeds.' (b) If status comes from deeds, then varna was about roles and functions, not birth.
s: (a) A brahmana by deeds, not birth
(b) Varna as functional, tied to roles

questions.q: Give two pieces of evidence from the chapter that women held a respected position in the Vedic period.
questions.a: Any two of: participation in scholarly learning, performing rituals alongside men, taking part in chariot races, attending the sabha, hymns attributed to women sages such as Apala, Vishvavara, Ghosha and Lopamudra, revered goddesses such as Usha and Aditi.

questions.q: The Tolkappiyam and the Pattinappalai both come from Sangam literature. Show how the second supports the idea that society was organised more by occupation than by rigid varna.
questions.a: The Pattinappalai describes a dynamic, trade-oriented society in which merchants, salt-makers, fishermen, artisans, agriculturists and warriors interacted actively, which suggests organisation by occupation and economic function; the Tolkappiyam's fourfold division was also premised on occupation and marked by fluidity.
s: The occupational groups the Pattinappalai describes
Conclusion: occupation and economic function, not rigid varna

questions.q: Explain how the four ashramas, in principle, benefit both the person and society.
questions.a: Dividing life into four stages with their respective dharmas provides fulfilment to a person in social, moral and spiritual aspects, and this leads to harmony and balance in society.
s: Fulfilment in social, moral and spiritual aspects

questions.q: Nisha says: 'Women's position declined after the Vedic age, so later women could not influence religion, governance or the economy.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says the position and roles of women fluctuated, even declined, with changing conditions. But she is wrong that they had no influence: Prabhavati Gupta ruled as a regent and issued land grants, Sembiyan Mahadevi supported temples, and Sangam women worked in agriculture and fishing.
s: The right part: position fluctuated and declined
The wrong part, with an example of women's influence

questions.q: The Rigveda verse reads: 'I am a poet; my father is a physician; my mother is a grinder of corn.' Answer the three questions a historian asks of a source: what does it tell us, what can we understand, and what might it not tell us?
questions.a: Evidence: the family has three occupations, poet, physician and corn grinder. Interpretation: occupations were flexible and not fixed by birth at that stage. Limits: it describes one family and does not tell us how common this was or about other regions or periods.
s: Limits: one family, not the whole society

questions.q: Explain three factors the chapter gives for the emergence of jati, and why the number of jatis kept increasing.
questions.a: Intermarriage among the varnas, migrating communities becoming endogamous and territorial differences. There was no restriction on the number of jatis, and new social groups and occupations kept developing, so the number grew.
s: Endogamy of migrating communities and territorial differences
No limit on number, new groups and occupations

questions.q: 'Varna and jati were not always rigid social categories.' Justify using at least three pieces of evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Rulers came from diverse social backgrounds, including the Nandas, Mauryas, Shungas, Satavahanas, Vakatakas, Guptas and Pushyabhutis. The Mandsaur inscription shows silk weavers moving and taking up other skills. The Karitalai plates record brahmanas as land managers. The Sutta Nipata says one is a brahmana by deeds. The Tolkappiyam and Pattinappalai suggest an occupation-based society. The Rigveda verse shows diverse occupations in a family.
s: Brahmanas as land managers in the Karitalai plates
The Sutta Nipata and the Sangam texts

questions.q: Describe the role and position of women in early Indian society from the Vedic period to the Chola period, showing both continuity and change.
questions.a: Vedic women took part in learning, rituals, chariot races and the sabha; hymns are attributed to women sages and goddesses were revered. The position fluctuated and even declined later, yet women kept contributing to household management, agriculture, crafts and religious practice. In the Gupta-Vakataka period women characters are shown as educated, and Prabhavati Gupta ruled as regent. Sangam women were active in agriculture and the economy, with poetesses such as Avvaiyar. Under the Cholas, Sembiyan Mahadevi supported temples.
s: The Chola example and a conclusion

questions.q:
A heritage club studies two inscriptions. The Mandsaur Stone Inscription (473 CE) records silk weavers moving from Lata in Gujarat to Dashapura in Madhya Pradesh and gaining other skills. The Karitalai copper plates of Maharaja Jayanatha record people of a particular varna managing land. The club can prepare only one display for the school fair.
(a) In which period does the chapter place the Mandsaur inscription?
(b) Name two skills besides weaving in which the guild was proficient.
(c) The Karitalai plates record which group as land managers?
(d) Which display would better show social mobility? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) The Gupta period. (b) Archery and astrology. (c) Brahmanas. (d) Mandsaur shows a whole guild moving and widening its skills; Karitalai shows a group usually linked with learning and ritual in an agricultural role. Either with a reason.
s: (d) A justified choice between the two displays

questions.q:
Mr Verma, 40, runs a cloth shop and supports his household. His father, 68, has handed over the shop and lives in a forest hut. His daughter, 15, is at a hostel studying. Mr Verma earns a good profit this year and must choose between expanding the shop and funding a small village school.
(a) Name the ashrama each of the three is in.
(b) Which purushartha is Mr Verma pursuing when he builds the shop's profit, and how must it be guided?
(c) His daughter says women in early India did not study. Correct her using the chapter.
(d) Should he expand the shop or fund the school? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Grihastha, vanaprastha and brahmacharya respectively. (b) Artha, guided by dharma, aligned with the welfare of society. (c) Women took part in scholarly learning and hymns are attributed to women sages. (d) Expansion creates jobs and secures the family; the school serves society's welfare as dharma asks. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (d) A justified choice between expansion and school

questions.q: Families in Bihar stand in the river at dawn to offer prayers to the sun at Chhath. How does the chapter explain such practices?
questions.a: They continue ancient practices rooted in dependence on nature. The chapter says Vedic deities were associated with elements such as the sun and rain, that sun worship during Chhath and Makar Sankranti continues some ancient practices, and that nature was viewed as sacred and powerful.
o: They continue ancient practices rooted in dependence on nature
They were introduced by the Bhakti saints of the 6th century in the Tamil region
They began when renunciants gave up the worship of nature
They replaced the Vedic worship of nature with the worship of personal deities

questions.q: In 6th-century Tamil country a devotee composes hymns in praise of Lord Shiva without elaborate rituals. To which group does the chapter assign such saint-poets?
questions.a: The Nayanmars, the Shaiva saint-poets. The chapter says the Nayanmars were the sixty-three Shaiva saint-poets, while the Alvars were twelve saint-poets praising Vishnu.
o: The Nayanmars, the Shaiva saint-poets
The Alvars, the twelve saint-poets of Vishnu
The shramanas, who strive and live by begging
The parivrajakas, who wander without shelter

questions.q: Why would the Bhakti path have appealed to a farmer's daughter who could not take part in elaborate yajnas?
questions.a: It offered direct devotion without elaborate rituals, open to all. The chapter describes Bhakti as a path that offered a direct connection with the gods without the elaborate rituals prescribed in the Vedas and was accessible to all, regardless of class or gender.
o: It offered direct devotion without elaborate rituals, open to all
It limited worship to scholars who had completed the gurukula
It required offerings to the sacred fire at every stage of life
It was confined to temples in the northern plains

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a feature of the gurukula system as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: Students avoided arts and physical training. The chapter says students were also trained in music, dance, painting, physical education and martial arts such as archery, so a Vedas-only course is not what it describes.
o: Students avoided arts and physical training
The student was treated as a member of the teacher's family
Students practised yoga and meditation and served the guru
Subjects included grammar, mathematics, medicine and astronomy

questions.q: Which of these shows that the idea of renunciation was already present in the Vedic tradition before Gautama Buddha and Mahavira?
questions.a: The vanaprastha and samnyasa stages. The chapter says that of the four ashramas, vanaprastha and samnyasa clearly have a renunciatory connotation.
o: The vanaprastha and samnyasa stages
The use of the term shramana in Buddhist texts
The organised Bhakti devotion of the Alvars
The sixteen rites of passage

questions.q:
Read the statements about religious life and learning.
1. The Alvars were sixty-three Shaiva saint-poets who composed hymns in praise of Lord Shiva.
2. The Bhakti tradition began in the 6th century CE and has no earlier reference in any text.
3. Each Vedic deity was associated with an element of nature such as the sun, rain, fire or earth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Statement 1 is false: the Alvars were twelve Vishnu saint-poets, and the sixty-three Nayanmars were Shaiva. Statement 2 is false: early references to Bhakti occur in the Mahabharata. Statement 3 is from the chapter.
o: 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bhakti was open to people of every class and gender.
Reason (R): Bhakti required the elaborate rituals prescribed in the Vedas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. A is true. R is false: the chapter says Bhakti offered a direct connection with the gods without the elaborate Vedic rituals, which is why it was open to all.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A retired householder, having completed grihastha, moves to live in the forest as the next of the four ashramas. He has entered ___.
questions.a: Vanaprastha

questions.q: (a) Name any two terms by which renunciants were known. (b) Which two stages of the ashramas already carried a renunciatory meaning?
questions.a: (a) Any two of parivrajaka (wanderer), bhikshu (one who lives by begging alms), shramana (one who strives). (b) Vanaprastha and samnyasa.
