questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say Vedic nature worship reflected about early societies? (b) Give one festival practice today that carries it forward.
questions.a: (a) Their dependence on nature for survival, so nature was seen as sacred and powerful, with a sense of respect and responsibility. (b) Sun worship during Chhath or on Makar Sankranti.
s: (a) Dependence on nature, so nature viewed as sacred

questions.q: Distinguish the Vedic way of approaching the divine from the Bhakti way, using the chapter.
questions.a: Vedic worship invoked deities through prayers and sacrificial rituals (yajnas) with offerings, often to the sacred fire. Bhakti offered a direct connection with personal deities such as Vishnu and Shiva, without elaborate rituals, open to all.
s: Vedic: prayers and yajnas with offerings
Bhakti: direct devotion, no elaborate rituals, open to all

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by the guru-shishya parampara, and how did it regard the teacher?
questions.a: The teacher-student relationship was regarded as sacred and close. The guru or acharya was highly respected and seen as a guide who helped students move from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge.
s: The teacher-student tradition as sacred and close
The teacher as guide from ignorance to knowledge

questions.q: Why does the chapter call education in early India a complete preparation for life, not just a path to a career? Give two supporting points.
questions.a: It cultivated inner values such as truth, patience and humility, and trained students in dharma and in practical skills, arts and crafts, yoga and meditation, along with the subjects of study.
s: Practical skills, arts, yoga and meditation

questions.q: Meena says: 'Even when kingdoms rose and fell, many Indian knowledge traditions kept going.' Check her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says that despite the rise and fall of kingdoms, many knowledge traditions and practices persisted. Evidence: foundational Sanskrit grammar by Panini, Pingala and Patanjali; medical classics, the Charakasamhita and Sushrutasamhita; and Tamil literature such as the Tirukkural and Sangam texts.
s: The chapter's statement that traditions persisted despite political change

questions.q: Compare a gurukula student's life with your own school life on any three of: daily routine, subjects, relationship with teachers, discipline, living arrangements.
questions.a: Example: living arrangement - the gurukula student lived in the teacher's home as a member of the family, while a day scholar goes home; subjects - Vedas, grammar, logic, mathematics, medicine plus arts and martial arts, while school follows a set curriculum; discipline - self-control and obedience in the gurukula.
s: First comparison with a gurukula fact

questions.q: Name three works or authors from the chapter's account of India's literary heritage, each from a different field, and say what field it belongs to.
questions.a: For example: Panini's Ashtadhyayi (Sanskrit grammar), the Charakasamhita (medicine), the Tirukkural (Tamil literature), Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha (Sanskrit poetry), Manusmriti (dharma and law).

questions.q: 'Education in early India was a complete preparation for life, not merely a path to a career.' Justify with evidence from the chapter on values, subjects, skills and the teacher-student bond.
questions.a: Values: truth, patience, regularity, humility, control of senses and purity of self. Subjects: the Vedas with grammar, logic, philosophy, ethics, mathematics, science, medicine and astronomy. Skills: music, dance, painting, physical education and archery, yoga, meditation and service to the guru. The guru-shishya bond was sacred and the student part of the teacher's family. Students were trained to live in accordance with dharma, with duties to parents, teachers and gods.
s: The arts, physical and practical training

questions.q: Trace the development of religious life in the chapter from the Vedic worship of nature, through the renunciants, to the Bhakti tradition.
questions.a: Vedic deities were linked to nature and invoked in yajnas with offerings to fire. Around the middle of the first millennium BCE renunciants (parivrajakas, bhikshus, shramanas) arose, including Buddha and Mahavira, though renunciation was already in the vanaprastha and samnyasa stages. Worship later centred on personal deities such as Vishnu, Shiva and Shakti. Bhakti offered a direct path accessible to all, with early references in the Mahabharata and organised growth in the 6th century Tamil region through the twelve Alvars and sixty-three Nayanmars.
s: The Alvars and Nayanmars in the 6th century

questions.q:
A school in Pune plans a model of an ancient seat of learning for its fair. The class picks the ruins of a large campus with housing, drainage and waste-management systems that attracted students from India and other regions. The model must fit on one table, so the class can build either the whole campus layout or a single gurukula hut with a teacher and students.
(a) Which centre's ruins does the description fit?
(b) Name two other centres of learning from the chapter's list.
(c) Name two practical or artistic subjects, besides the Vedas, that gurukula students learnt.
(d) Which model better tells the story of early Indian learning? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) Takshashila. (b) Any two of Nalanda, Vikramshila, Vallabhi, Odantapuri, etc. named in the chapter's map. (c) Any two of music, dance, painting, physical education, archery, mathematics, medicine. (d) The campus shows organised higher learning; the hut shows the close teacher-student bond. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (d) A justified choice between campus and hut

questions.q:
A school choir plans an evening on the Bhakti saint-poets of the 6th-century Tamil region, who praised Vishnu and Shiva. The evening is 75 minutes long. The choir has to decide whether to sing one verse from every saint-poet, at 1 minute each, or three verses from a chosen set of 25, at 3 minutes each.
(a) How many saint-poets did the Alvars and Nayanmars together make up?
(b) Work out how long it would take to sing one verse from each at 1 minute each.
(c) Why did Bhakti spread to people who did not perform elaborate rituals?
(d) Which plan should the choir follow? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) 12 + 63 = 75. (b) 75 x 1 = 75 minutes, which exactly fills the evening; the second plan is 25 x 3 = 75 minutes too. (c) It offered a direct connection with the gods without elaborate rituals and was open to all regardless of class or gender. (d) The first plan shows breadth, with every poet heard; the second shows depth. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (c) Direct, no elaborate rituals, open to all
(d) A justified choice between breadth and depth

questions.q: A pious donor in the 2nd century CE wants his gift to give a monastery a steady yearly income. Which arrangement from the Nashik cave inscription would suit him?
questions.a: Depositing it with guilds that pay a fixed rate of interest. The Nashik inscription records donations deposited with guilds that were obligated to pay a fixed rate of interest, which was used to maintain Buddhist monasteries and caves.
o: Depositing it with guilds that pay a fixed rate of interest
Burying the sum in the cave so that it stays safe
Lending the sum to the king in return for a share of the harvest
Spending the sum at once on cloth for the monks

questions.q: A buyer in a Mauryan-age market finds that the salt she bought was mixed with sand. What does the chapter say about how the state handled such trade?
questions.a: It acted to prevent adulteration and protect consumers. The chapter says the state ensured the safety of trade routes, took measures to prevent adulteration of goods and protect consumers from unfair practices, and strictly regulated salt production.
o: It acted to prevent adulteration and protect consumers
It left all trade to the guilds and did not regulate anything
It allowed anyone to make and sell salt freely
It fixed the price of every commodity and banned private trade

questions.q: A potter in a guild sells poor pots and breaks the guild's rules. Which body in the chapter's account supervised the conduct of the guild's members?
questions.a: The guild courts, which enforced discipline. The chapter says the conduct of guild members was supervised through guild courts that enforced professional standards and discipline.
o: The guild courts, which enforced discipline
The village assemblies, which collected the tax on land
The council of ministers, which advised the king
The Sabha, which heard disputes in the Vedic age

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in the chapter as a major port of early India?
questions.a: Pataliputra, an early historical city. The chapter names Muziris, Kaveripattinam, Arikamedu and Masulipatnam as major ports.
o: Pataliputra, an early historical city
Muziris, a port on the western coast
Kaveripattinam, a port on the Tamil coast
Arikamedu, a port on the Tamil coast

questions.q: Villagers near Kallanai find that a dam built many centuries ago still serves their fields. What does the chapter say about the Grand Anicut that explains this?
questions.a: It stored water, supported farming and was repaired later. The chapter says the Grand Anicut built by Karikala Chola helped store and distribute water, supported agriculture and encouraged settlements, was repaired by later rulers and remains in use today.
o: It stored water, supported farming and was repaired later
It was built by Pushyagupta, a governor appointed by Chandragupta Maurya
It was a canal that served only Muziris and the Roman trade
It was a temple tank managed by a Chola village assembly

questions.q:
Read the statements about the early Indian economy.
1. The basic tax on land was a fixed proportion of the produce, generally one-sixth.
2. Guilds functioned as banks, financiers and trustees as well as associations of craftspersons.
3. The Nashik cave inscription records deposits with guilds that paid a fixed rate of interest.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. All three statements are from the chapter: the land tax was generally one-sixth, guilds acted as banks, financiers and trustees, and the Nashik cave inscription records interest-bearing deposits.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The early Indian state took an active interest in building and keeping up irrigation works.
Reason (R): Agriculture was one of the major sources of revenue for the state.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and R explains A: the chapter says facilitating agriculture remained a major preoccupation of the state because it was one of the major sources of revenue.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each item with what the chapter says about it.
1. Sudarshana Lake dam
2. Grand Anicut (Kallanai)
3. Nashik cave inscription
4. Sanchi gateway inscription
a. Built by Karikala Chola and still in use today
b. Built by Pushyagupta, a governor appointed by Chandragupta Maurya
c. Records interest-bearing deposits with guilds
d. Refers to the welfare activities of the guild of ivory workers from Vidisha
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c, 4-d. The Sudarshana dam is credited to Pushyagupta; the Grand Anicut to Karikala Chola; the Nashik inscription records deposits with guilds; the Sanchi gateway inscription mentions the ivory workers' guild of Vidisha.

questions.q: A Mauryan farmer harvests 4,800 kg of grain and the state takes the generally prevalent one-sixth. The tax is ___ kg.
True or False: The Nashik cave inscription shows that guilds could receive deposits and pay a fixed rate of interest on them. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The inscription records that monetary donations were deposited with professional guilds, which were obligated to pay a fixed rate of interest, used to maintain Buddhist monasteries and caves. This shows guilds also worked as banking and credit institutions.
s: Reason: deposits with guilds earned fixed interest, so guilds acted as banks

questions.q: (a) Name the two major land routes that had emerged by about the 6th century BCE. (b) How did they connect inland regions with the coast?
questions.a: (a) Dakshinapatha and Uttarapatha. (b) They linked inland regions with coastal ports, integrating overland and maritime trade systems.
s: (b) Linked inland regions with coastal ports, joining overland and maritime trade

questions.q: (a) Who built a dam on Sudarshana Lake near Girnar, and who appointed him? (b) Why does the chapter say the state cared about such works?
questions.a: (a) Pushyagupta, a governor appointed by Chandragupta Maurya. (b) Facilitating agriculture was a major preoccupation of the state because agriculture was one of its major sources of revenue.
s: (b) Agriculture as a major source of revenue

questions.q: Give two ways in which guilds protected buyers and artisans, according to the chapter.
questions.a: They regulated the quality of goods and often fixed prices; their members' conduct was supervised through guild courts.

questions.q: Name two commodities from the Chera region of Sangam literature and the crop the chapter links to the Deccan's black soil.
questions.a: Any two of jackfruit, pepper, turmeric (also ragi and sugarcane); the Deccan's black soil was suitable for cotton.
s: Cotton for the black soil of the Deccan

questions.q: Dev says: 'Early states had little to do with trade; merchants managed everything on their own.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says well-structured states provided the infrastructure and conditions for trade. The state ensured the safety of trade routes, took measures to prevent adulteration and protect consumers, and strictly regulated salt production.
s: The state provided infrastructure and safe routes
It regulated goods, adulteration and salt production

questions.q: A donor deposits 3,000 kahapanas, 2,000 with one weavers' guild and 1,000 with another. Suppose the first pays 1 kahapana per 100 each month and the second 3/4 kahapana per 100 each month. Work out the monthly interest from each guild and the total.
questions.a: First guild: 2,000/100 x 1 = 20. Second guild: 1,000/100 x 0.75 = 7.5. Total 27.5 kahapanas per month.

questions.q: Give three reasons why irrigation works such as dams and canals were important enough to be recorded in inscriptions.
questions.a: They supported agriculture, which sustained rural livelihoods and was a major source of state revenue; they stored and distributed water and encouraged the growth of settlements; and they lasted for centuries, needing repair by later rulers.
s: Stored water, encouraged settlements and lasted for centuries

questions.q: Explain how trade routes, ports and guilds together supported the economy of early India.
questions.a: The Dakshinapatha and Uttarapatha linked regions and connected inland areas with ports such as Muziris, Kaveripattinam, Arikamedu and Masulipatnam, uniting overland and maritime trade. By the early centuries CE, trade with Rome grew by sea and overland via Central Asia. Guilds of traders, artisans and merchants expanded commerce, regulated quality, fixed prices and worked as banks. Silver punch-marked coins circulated. The Jataka mentions eighteen types of guilds, showing their strength.

questions.q: 'Agriculture was the backbone of the early Indian economy and a constant concern of the state.' Justify with evidence on land revenue, crops and irrigation.
questions.a: The basic land tax was generally one-sixth of the produce. Land was classified for revenue assessment and the Arthashastra describes types of village land. Many crops are listed, including rice, pulses, wheat, sugarcane and cotton in the Deccan. The Milindapanho describes eight stages of farming. Irrigation works such as the Sudarshana dam and the Grand Anicut were built and maintained because agriculture was a major source of revenue. Together these show the state's concern.

questions.q:
Rudra, a farmer in a Mauryan village, harvests 4,800 kg of grain. The state takes its usual share. He sells the remaining grain at 25 kahapanas per 100 kg and deposits half of the money with a weavers' guild that pays 1 kahapana per 100 each month. He is also thinking of spending the deposit instead on repairing the channel that waters his field.
(a) What proportion of the produce does the chapter say the state generally took?
(b) How much grain does the state take and how much is left to sell?
(c) How much interest does the deposit earn in one month?
(d) Should Rudra keep the deposit with the guild or spend it on the channel? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) One-sixth. (b) 4,800 / 6 = 800 kg to the state; 4,000 kg left. (c) 4,000 / 100 x 25 = 1,000 kahapanas; half is 500; 500 / 100 x 1 = 5 kahapanas a month. (d) The guild gives steady income and acts as a bank; the channel supports the crops, as the chapter notes irrigation is closely tied to agriculture. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (d) A justified choice between deposit and channel

questions.q:
A weavers' guild in the textile centre of Mathura fixes the price and quality of its cloth. A new member sells cloth below the fixed price, using poor yarn. Some members want to expel him; others want the guild court to warn him first. The guild also holds a deposit from a donor, whose interest maintains a monastery.
(a) Which body in the guild would examine the new member's conduct?
(b) Name two other roles of guilds, apart from regulating quality and prices.
(c) Which role does the deposit from the donor show?
(d) Should the guild expel him or warn him first? Give a point for each and decide.
questions.a: (a) The guild court. (b) Any two of: acting as banks, financiers and trustees. (c) The role of a bank or credit institution, investing funds and paying interest. (d) Expulsion protects the guild's standards and buyers; a warning gives the member a chance to correct and keeps a skilled weaver. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (d) A justified choice between expulsion and warning
